newsitem.title: JAPAN: E.Asian Grain - Japan buys corn as premiums ease.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - Japan buys corn as premiums ease.

text.p: U.S. corn premiums have eased on a fall in trans-Pacific freight rates and this is underpinning Japanese imports, Tokyo traders said on Monday.
"The freight rates recovered last week. But then a technical downward correction emerged," one corn trader said.
Tokyo dealers quoted U.S. corn premiums at about 100 U.S. cents a bushel C&F over Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) March futures, against nearly 103 cents a week ago.
Japanese importers said they had now covered more than 50 percent of their U.S. corn requirements for January to March, 1997 shipment and that they would remain in the market this week.
The Japanese Agriculture Ministry said on Friday it would release up to 400,000 tonnes of corn and up to 300,000 tonnes of barley from national feed grain stocks in the September to November period.

The decision was taken due to expected delayed shipments in corn and barley during this period, mainly from the United States, because of historically low U.S. grain stocks, a senior ministry official said.
"There was growing concern about delayed grain shipments, particularly between September and November, because of historically low stocks in the U.S. and tighter supply/demand," one corn trader said.
In the oilseeds market, Japanese importers said they had already bought nearly 150,000 tonnes of U.S. soybeans for October shipment and expected to continue buying this week.
Another corn trader said freight premiums to South Korea remained unchanged from last week at between $22-$23 a tonne from the U.S. Gulf and $13-$14 from the Pacific Northwest.
In the wheat market, South Korean feed millers were likely to buy one or two cargoes of Canadian feed wheat for shipment in November, a trader at a major feed mill firm said.
He said sellers were currently offering Canadian feed wheat at $168 a tonne C&F.
U.S. soybean premiums were quoted at about 120 U.S. cents a bushel C&F over CBOT January futures.
In South Korea, corn importers continued to withold purchases as they had mostly covered their requirements through to February shipment, local traders said.
"There has been no change in the domestic market. Most buyers will take a wait-and-see attitude unless corn prices fall to around $160-$165 (C&F) a tonne," one trader said.
U.S. corn was quoted at $175 a tonne C&F South Korea this week versus $173 a week ago.
